title: Knowledge as worship
hookLine: whoever takes a path seeking knowledge, Allah makes easy a path to the garden (Muslim)

cards: Dark streets before dawn. A student with a borrowed book under one arm walks across the city to sit in a teacher's circle. The walk is long, and nobody will remember it.
Except, says a hadith, it counts. Muslim records the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, saying that whoever takes a path seeking knowledge, Allah makes easy for him, by it, a path to the garden.
Not only the lesson: the path to the lesson. The walk itself is pointed somewhere. Today, our last day with the Abbasids and the House of Wisdom.

teach.h: MY LORD! INCREASE ME IN KNOWLEDGE.
teach.b: The Qur'an keeps knowledge close to prayer. It gives a short plea to say, in Pickthall's translation: "My Lord! Increase me in knowledge." And it asks: "Are those who know equal with those who know not?"

And the same hadith in Muslim goes on: when people gather in a house of God, reciting the Book and studying it together, tranquility comes down on them and mercy covers them. Study, in a mosque, as a kind of prayer.
Which knowledge? Here scholars read differently. Some say the hadith means first of all knowledge of the religion: the Qur'an, the Sunnah, how to pray and live rightly.
Others widen it to any useful knowledge sought with a good intention, the healing that helps the sick, the arithmetic that divides an inheritance fairly.
Both readings agree on this much: the seeking itself can be devotion.

teach.h: LOOKING BACK OVER THE HOUSE OF WISDOM.
teach.b: Now look back over the road since the House of Wisdom. Al-Khwarizmi restoring and balancing. Zero arriving from India.
Hospitals that cared for all who came. Al-Biruni measuring the earth, Ibn al-Haytham testing what he thought he knew.
Astronomers working out the hours of prayer. Al-Jahiz staring at ants, copyists on the booksellers' street, al-Bukhari sifting reports, the imams teaching in their circles.
Different people, different fields, and for some of them the same conviction underneath: learning is something you can offer. Tomorrow we cross the sea to a new land.

how: Muslims may begin study by setting an intention for God, and study circles meet in mosques and homes to read and discuss the Qur'an and hadith together.

games.q: you're a student in Baghdad. to hear one lesson you walk across the city before dawn, every day. what is the walk, in the light of the hadith?
o: wasted time; only the lesson counts.
part of it: a path toward the garden.
worth it only if you become a well-known scholar.
games.why: the hadith speaks of whoever takes a path seeking knowledge. the walking itself is part of what is made easy toward the garden.

practice: Ask yourself one honest question: what's one small thing I'd like to understand better, a verse, a word, how something works, a skill someone close to me needs?
Then think about why you want to know it, the way al-Bukhari's book begins with intention.
If you pray, you can offer this small bit of learning to God with the Qur'an's own words, my Lord, increase me in knowledge; if not, let the intention be the good it might do.

wordCard.voice: Ilm. Arabic for knowledge, kept close to prayer in the Qur'an and hadith: whoever takes a path seeking it, Allah makes easy for him a path to the garden. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: knowledge; the root also gives 'alim, one who knows, a scholar.

carryVoice: Your line: a path to the garden. The walk to the lesson counts too. See you tomorrow.
